name: Blood type diet

lead: The blood type diet, from naturopath Peter D'Adamo's 1996 book Eat Right 4 Your Type, tells people to eat according to their ABO blood group: a high-protein plan for type O, mostly plant-based for A, dairy-inclusive for B and a mix for AB. Followers adopt it to lose weight, improve digestion and energy, and reduce inflammation, which they link to a leaner physique and better-looking skin.

Research has examined it directly. A 2013 systematic review found no studies showing blood-type-specific benefits, and a 2018 analysis of 973 overweight adults found improvements in some markers tracked adherence to a given diet regardless of the participant's blood type.

paras: Followers get their blood group, then follow lists of 'beneficial', 'neutral' and 'avoid' foods for it, with matching exercise suggestions. Results depend on the underlying food pattern, such as more vegetables or less processed food.

The diet is not medically risky for most healthy people, but cutting whole food groups such as dairy or grains for no individual reason can narrow nutrient intake, a point dietitians raise. People with medical conditions typically consult their clinician.

social.title: Blood type diet – Lack of Evidence

chain: Eat more whole foods and fewer processed foods
Weight and body composition may change
angle.text: Followers use the diet to lose fat and improve energy and digestion, which they connect to appearance. Researchers attribute measured improvements to the foods eaten rather than to blood type.

lead: The blood type diet is an eating plan proposed by naturopathic physician Peter J. D'Adamo in his 1996 book Eat Right 4 Your Type. It links a person's ABO group to which foods are said to suit them, with claims of weight loss, better digestion, higher energy and lower disease risk.[1][2]

Followers use it as a body-composition and health framework. D'Adamo's premise is that lectins in food react with blood-type antigens, and each plan is tied to a supposed stage of human evolution: type O as hunter-gatherer, A as agrarian, B as nomadic and AB as a recent blend.[1][2]

The diet has been tested. A 2013 systematic review in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition found only one eligible article out of 1,415 screened references and none showing blood-type-specific effects.[3] Later Toronto studies found cardiometabolic improvements from adherence to certain blood-type diets, but these did not depend on the participant's blood type.[4][5]
infobox: About 7 million (as reported in a 2018 study)

paras: Foods are classed for each blood type as beneficial, neutral or avoid. Type O is directed to high-protein, low-carbohydrate eating that excludes grains and dairy; type A to a vegetarian pattern; type B to a balanced plan with dairy; and AB to a hybrid.[1][2] Exercise suggestions are also given, such as intense activity for O and calming practices like yoga for A.[1]

Sources trace the idea to the 1950s and 1960s observations of D'Adamo's father, naturopath James D'Adamo, who noticed patients responded differently to diets by blood type.[1][2] Peter D'Adamo popularised it with the 1996 book, which a 2018 paper reports sold about 7 million copies in over 60 languages.[4]

Critics, including dietitians and physicians, say the lectin and evolution premises are unsupported. Wikipedia notes the British Dietetic Association listed it among celebrity diets to avoid in 2019, and that the claim that type O is the ancestral blood group is disputed.[2] Norwegian medical journal commentaries from 2001 and 2002 also debated it.[6]
Cleveland Clinic experts quoted in a summary say benefits likely come from whole foods and reduced processed food rather than blood type.[1]
The 2013 systematic review found no studies directly testing whether following a blood-type diet improves health in people grouped by blood type.[3]

A 2014 PLOS ONE study of ABO genotype and blood-type diets found associations with cardiometabolic risk factors that did not depend on genotype.[7] A 2018 Journal of Nutrition secondary analysis of 973 overweight adults in the Toronto Healthy Diet Study found, for example, lower diastolic blood pressure with higher adherence to the type A diet, with ABO genotype not modifying the associations.[4] A 2022 study of 329 blood donors examined smoking, alcohol, caffeine and nutrient intake by blood group and found differences in intake habits.[5]

timeline.event: James D'Adamo observes diet responses by blood type in his clinics.[1]
Peter D'Adamo publishes Eat Right 4 Your Type.[1][2]
